text: Lessons seventeen and eighteen covered RACI and executive sponsorship — the structure of governance communication. This lesson is about the actual words — the part that trips up even well-staffed programs.

"Data governance" is part of the problem. To a business audience, "data" sounds like a tactical IT concern, and "governance" sounds like bureaucracy — rules on top of work that was going fine without them. None of this course's substance survives if the first sentence makes someone tune out.

Have one jargon-free sentence ready. Data governance is the rules, roles, and responsibilities for how data gets created, stored, accessed, and used — so the numbers people rely on are accurate, consistent, and there when they're needed. No metadata, no lineage, no framework names, unless you translate the term first.

The single biggest shift is framing. "You can't access this data anymore" becomes "here's the faster, approved way to get it." "This policy restricts what you can do" becomes "this is what makes the self-service dashboard safe to roll out." Same program — only one version gets a willing audience.

Match the channel to the audience. All-staff for the whole organization, with the sponsor visibly behind it. Manager briefings so people leaders can answer their own teams. Office hours and embedded stewards for day-to-day users. And one-on-ones, sponsor-led, for a specific skeptical stakeholder.

A plain sentence, enabler framing, the right channel, and real evidence from a pilot if you have it — that's how governance actually gets heard. Next up: the final lesson — pulling every chapter of this course together into one case study.
